webpage.description: Boris Vallejo is an epic fantasy painter, who has had an immense influence on fantasy book covers, computer game box art, and even the demoscene. Throughout the decades, his works have often been replicated by pixel artists, leading to controversy. I rediscovered Vallejo's great work for myself, looked into the demoscene's love for his pictures and decided to recreate one of his paintings using only four colors and record it on video. My little article here features fantasy art history, demoscene drama, and a lot of pixel art fun.

Como  eu consegui fazer dumps bons da maincpu do kn5000 esse mês usando o Arduino ligado na porta paralela, agora estou me preparando psicologicamente para encarar o desafio de fazer o dump da subcpu por técnicas similares.

um caminho possível que andei pensando é o seguinte:

* Mudar o ponto no qual eu insiro código arbitrário durante o boot para ser um pouco depois da rotina que carrega o payload executável para a subcpu.
* fazer um patch para que esse payload contenha código que lê os bytes de 0xFE0000 até 0xFFFFFF (que é onde fica a ROM de boot, com 128k bytes) e os envia para a maincpu por meio dos latches de comunicação inter-CPUs
* no código inserido durante o boot da maincpu, ficar lendo do latch e escrevendo na porta paralela.

Mas eu tenho um receio. Toda vez que esses latches recebem escrita de dado,  é gerada uma interrupção na CPU de destino da mensagem. E eu acho que eu teria que desabilitar essa rotina de tratamento de interrupção, caso contrário ela atrapalharia a minha recepção normal do dump.

E outro caminho possível seria eu fazer uso dessa rotina de tratamento de interrupção para receber o dump também. Mas... não sei se mexer nela não atrapalharia o protocolo inicial de carga do payload executável.

Então me parece que o caminho melhor seria eu dar uma estudada no disasm desse int handler e tentar me familiarizar com o protocolo em questão.

mas também existe a possibilidade do envio de payload não envolver a rotina de recepção de dados no lado da maincpu. E aí daria pra eu "estragar" essa int handler numa boa com um patch mais grosseiro mesmo

Tem um agravante, entretanto... Essa comunicação inter-CPU é feita por operações de "micro-dma" que o TLCS900 suporta. E tem algumas escritas em registradores de controle que não  estão sendo decodificadas corretamente pelo meu disassembler e suspeito que sejam relacionadas ao setup dessa micro-dma. Pra eu entender exatamente como funciona o protocolo de envio de payload para a subcpu seria importante eu consertar esse decoding dos opcodes extra dessa CPU. E não achei em lugar nenhum documentação dos valores desses opcodes, então estou no escuro.
ACHO que já troquei uma dessas instruções por NOP e o resultado, se não me falha a memória, foi de falha na inicialização da subcpu, por isso que acho que é relacionado ao setup de micro-dma

text.text: C64 Gets A Graphics Upgrade Courtesy Of Your Favorite Piano Manufacturer

texts.text: The Commodore 64 was quite a machine in its time, though a modern assessment would say that it’s severely lacking in the graphical department. [Vossi] has whipped up a bit of an upgrade for the C64 and C128, in the form of

text.text: a graphics expansion card running Yamaha hardware

As you might expect, the expansion is designed to fit neatly into a C64 cartridge slot. The card runs the Yamaha V9958—the video display processor known for its appearance in the MSX2+ computers. In this case, it’s paired with a healthy 128 kB of video RAM so it can really do its thing. The V9958 has an analog RGB output that can be set for PAL or NTSC operation, and can perform at resolutions up to 512×212 or even 512×424 interlaced. Naturally, it needs to be hooked directly up to a compatible screen, like a 1084, or one with SCART input. [Vossi] took the time to create some demos of the chip’s capabilities, drawing various graphics in a way that the C64 couldn’t readily achieve on its own.

texts.text: It’s a build that almost feels like its from an alternate universe, where Yamaha decided to whip up a third-party graphics upgrade for the C64. That didn’t happen, but

text.text: stranger team ups have occurred

texts.text: over the years.

text.text: [Thanks to Stephen Walters for the tip!]

text.text: (Image credit: Nintendo)
The official Nintendo Museum appears to be emulating SNES games on a Windows PC, which is slightly embarrassing

texts.text: Nintendo has had a difficult relationship with emulation, and that's putting it mildly. The company has often legally pursued

text.text: emulator developers

texts.text: and

text.text: ROM websites

texts.text: , and its website makes it clear that

text.text: it's not ok to copy or download older titles

texts.text: , nor download a ROM for emulation even if you own the original game, lest you fall foul of various copyright laws.
Twitter user

text.text: @ChrisMack32

texts.text: , however, seems to have made a rather embarrassing discovery. They've posted a video of a SNES controller being disconnected (via USB, no less) from a booth at the official Nintendo Museum in Japan, and it turns out it makes a rather familiar noise—the

text.text: "ding dong dun"

texts.text: of a Windows USB device disconnect.
Hmm. While we only get a brief look at the screen, it appears whatever device the controller was connected to seems to be playing Super Mario World.

text.text: That's a SNES title

texts.text: , of course—which suggests that its being emulated on a Windows PC underneath.
Well, it is the superior machine, of course. Still, for a company that

text.text: has keenly banged the drum against emulators

texts.text: and sites distributing ROMS—even if they're used by those that own an original copy of the games they wish to emulate—it does seem a bit rich. Nintendo has even argued that emulation

text.text: "harms innovation"

texts.text: , which also seems like a bit of a stretch.
On the other hand, what did we really expect? A proper SNES running in every booth at the Nintendo Museum? Sounds like a nightmare to maintain, to me. You could always

text.text: run them officially on the Nintendo Switch

texts.text: of course, to keep things above board.

text.text: But that's a Windows sound effect for sure, so unless this video's been edited, it looks like the Nintendo Museum may have taken the easy route and booted them up on a good old fashioned PC, via an emulator.

And that's sort of the whole point, isn't it? While ROMs and emulators exist in the minds of many in a sort of moral grey area, I don't think I'd be blowing too many minds if I said that people are drawn to them for the sheer convenience, among other things. It's just, y'know, not actually legal.

text.text: As several Twitter users pointed out, the fact the controller was easily disconnected also means that, thanks to that open USB cable, this particular machine could now be connected to by any number of devices—and thereby very easily compromised.

So, a fail on the emulation front, and a cybersecurity whoopsie all in one go. Good stuff. Anyways, one simple little sound effect, one slightly embarrassing reveal. I could hark on about this being a massive tacit win for the PC and emulation as a whole, but it seems in poor taste at this point. I think someone at the Nintendo Museum may be about to receive a nasty letter, and that's enough to ruin anyone's day.
